cards.title: Google DeepMind Open-Sources WeatherNext: Cyclone Forecasting Model That Adds One Day of Predictive Accuracy
cards.why_it_matters: A published Nature result with real operational deployment and open-source release is a landmark for ML-in-science; the architecture choices — co-training on 20TB atmospheric data plus IBTrACS, using Functional Generative Networks for ensembles — are technically instructive for applied ML researchers.
cards.summary: WeatherNext, published in Nature, achieves state-of-the-art cyclone track, intensity, and wind-structure prediction. Its 3-day forecasts match what prior models achieved at 2 days — roughly a decade of meteorological progress. The model uses Functional Generative Networks (FGNs), trains on ~20TB of atmospheric data and ~5,000 historical storms (IBTrACS), and generates a 15-day forecast in under a minute on a TPU. WeatherNext 2 and WeatherNext Cyclones are now open-sourced.

cards.title: Baseten Joins Hugging Face Inference Providers with Support for DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM Models
cards.why_it_matters: Gives you a direct, low-friction path to run frontier open-weight models like DeepSeek V4 Flash via HF's router or your own Baseten key, with zero extra markup on routed requests.
cards.summary: Baseten is now a supported Inference Provider on the HF Hub, enabling serverless access to models including Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4 Flash, and GLM-5.2 for conversational and text-generation tasks. Accessible via huggingface_hub (>=1.26.1) and @huggingface/inference JS SDK. Routed requests pass through HF with no added markup; direct requests bill to your Baseten account.

cards.title: Domain Expertise Is the Key Multiplier When Using LLMs, Not Prompting Tricks
cards.why_it_matters: As an AI/research engineer who both builds and uses LLMs, understanding where the human remains the bottleneck — and why — is directly relevant to how you structure your own workflows and evaluate model capability claims.
cards.summary: The author argues that LLMs equalize novices but amplify experts: domain knowledge lets users steer models harder, identify wrong outputs, and suggest better directions — illustrated by Terence Tao's ChatGPT session on the Jacobian Conjecture counterexample. The limiting factor for many tasks is the human's ability to specify what a good solution looks like, not the model's knowledge.
